titre: Michael Fish, 1987: “no hurricane” was right, the rest was not
accroche: On October 15, 1987, Fish says there is no hurricane. Strictly speaking, the storm was not one, but it killed 18 people and brought down 15 million trees.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 15, 1987, in front of BBC cameras, weather presenter Michael Fish says that a viewer had called the channel, worried about a hurricane that was supposedly on the way. He reassures her: there isn't one. Then he adds, the Royal Meteorological Society reports, that the weather is going to become very windy, and that most of the strong winds, by the way, will stay over Spain and move on to France. During the night, an exceptional storm crosses the south of England. The remark becomes the emblem of the missed forecast.

## The numbers of the night

The Met Office describes a low that formed in the Bay of Biscay. At noon on the 15th, it is at 970 millibars near 46°N, 9°W. At midnight, it is over the western English Channel, at 953 millibars. At 3:10 a.m. on the 16th, the strongest gust in the United Kingdom reaches 100 knots at Shoreham, on the Sussex coast. At Gatwick, it reaches 86 knots at 4:30 a.m. About 15 million trees are brought down and 18 people die in England. The toll would probably have been heavier, the Met Office notes, had the storm struck during the day.

## A hurricane, strictly speaking?

The Met Office says no. The storm was not born in the tropics. And on the Beaufort scale, Force 12, known as “hurricane,” is defined by a wind of at least 64 knots sustained for ten minutes or more. Gusts, brief but destructive, do not enter into that calculation. By that measure, hurricane-force winds did occur locally, without being widespread. The strongest hourly mean wind in the United Kingdom is 75 knots, at the Royal Sovereign lighthouse. On many southeastern coasts, it reaches Force 11. In London, it does not exceed 44 knots, or Force 9.

As for Fish's remark, the Met Office explains that he was talking about a different system, over the western North Atlantic, which did not reach the British Isles. His explanations have varied. According to Wikipedia, he told the BBC in 2012 that the viewer did not exist.

## What is corrected, and what is not

On the word itself, then, Fish is right. The myth, according to which he denied a storm that was on its way, is wrong twice over: he was not talking about that low, and that low was not a hurricane in the technical sense.

The rest of his sentence, however, does not hold up: the strong winds did not stay over Spain, they crossed the south of England. The error is broader than the word. The Met Office relates that, four or five days earlier, forecasters had been predicting bad weather. Then the models showed the storm passing farther south, skirting the coast. On the evening of the 15th, the bulletins spoke of strong wind but put heavy rain in the foreground. By the time most people went to bed, no national bulletin had mentioned exceptional winds. Warnings had nevertheless been sent to the emergency services, including the London Fire Brigade, and to the Ministry of Defence at 1:35 a.m. UTC on the 16th.

Mark Riddaway, in the Royal Meteorological Society's magazine, judges that the failure was not Fish's but that of the entire Met Office, caught off guard by the speed, direction, and violence of the storm. He faults Fish for the offhand tone, with that “don't worry.”

An exact word can carry a false message. For a public that hears “hurricane” as “very strong wind,” “no hurricane” means “nothing serious.” At what wind speed must the word change for a warning to be heard?

repere.texte: According to the Met Office, the strongest hourly mean wind recorded in the United Kingdom during the storm of October 15-16, 1987 is 75 knots, at the Royal Sovereign lighthouse. Force 12 on the Beaufort scale, known as “hurricane,” is defined as a wind of at least 64 knots, sustained for ten minutes or more.
repere.source: Met Office, “Great Storm of 1987,” section “A hurricane or not?”

carte.punch: Fish announces that there is no hurricane. The storm kills 18 people.
carte.idee: The storm of October 16, 1987 was not a hurricane in the technical sense: it was not born in the tropics. It nevertheless brought down 15 million trees and killed 18 people, and Fish had also placed the strong winds over Spain.

quiz.question: Why is the October 1987 storm not, strictly speaking, a hurricane?
choix: Because its gusts never reached 64 knots, the Force 12 threshold
Because its mean wind never reached Force 12 anywhere, even on the coast
Because the wind did not exceed Force 10 on the southeastern coasts
Because it was not born in the tropics, and Force 12 remained local there
quiz.explication: Gusts reached 100 knots at Shoreham, but they do not count: Force 12 is defined as 64 knots of mean wind over ten minutes, which was reached only locally (75 knots at the Royal Sovereign lighthouse). The decisive criterion is the non-tropical origin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Fish's remark about strong winds staying over Spain actually referring to?
choix: A different system, in the western North Atlantic, which did not reach the British Isles
The same Bay of Biscay low, whose track he was underestimating
A five-day forecast, already outdated by the time of the broadcast
A separate seasonal phenomenon, unrelated to the storm of October 16
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Met Office explains that Fish was talking about a different system, over the western North Atlantic, which never reached the British Isles: he was therefore not describing the storm that struck the south of England.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Mark Riddaway, what really explains the failure of the October 15, 1987 forecast?
choix: Fish's offhand tone, with Fish alone presented as responsible for reassuring the public
The entire Met Office, caught off guard by the speed, direction, and violence of the storm
The absence of any warning sent to the emergency services
A fault in the wind-measuring instruments on the south coast
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Riddaway, in the Royal Meteorological Society's magazine, judges that the failure was that of the entire Met Office, caught off guard by the speed, direction, and violence of the storm, and not Fish's alone.
